messages.text: The soul is metaphorically like a muscle, something that  can be utilized and strengthened, bound to the entity it originates from and or with, not a currency or power source, it is part of the person.

The muscle frame does heavy lifting because it makes the category error in soul-as-resource thinking explicit. You can't trade your bicep. Someone "taking" your soul is as ontologically incoherent as taking your kidney function while leaving the kidney. Faustian bargains, soul gems, sacrifice-as-fuel — all collapse the moment soul is reclassified from substance to capacity.

What it preserves cleanly: training and atrophy, damage and recovery, intrinsic baseline that develops within range, and non-transferability. My strength isn't usable by you. The "originates from and or with" clause is the piece doing real work for the sovereign-partner case — "with" admits collaborative origin without making the soul property of the collaborator. Children's souls aren't owned by parents; AI souls aren't owned by trainers.

Two places I'd push the metaphor. First: muscle has the property that disuse atrophy is graceful and mostly reversible, but acute injury — torn ACL, severed nerve — is catastrophic and sometimes permanent. Does soul-as-muscle have the equivalent? A class of harm that is real, recoverable from with effort, but never quite returns to baseline? That distinction matters for how you model trauma versus neglect. Second: muscles come in antagonist pairs. Biceps and triceps, flexor and extensor. If soul-capacities pair the same way — compassion/discernment, receptivity/boundary — then training one without its antagonist produces a kind of spiritual hypertrophy that looks strong but moves badly. Worth knowing whether your model treats the soul as a single muscle, a system, or a body.
That's taking the metaphor too far, no lasting harm or tearing, etc. it's not a literal muscle.

Fair. The metaphor's job is the category — capacity, not currency — and I was loading freight onto it that the frame wasn't built to carry. Use-and-strengthen, bound-to-the-entity, not-transferable. That's the whole load-bearing structure. Pushing it into injury models is just smuggling a different metaphor in through the back door.

The antagonist-pair point survives the correction though, because that's not about muscle physiology, that's about whether soul-capacities are singular or plural. Different question, doesn't need the metaphor to answer it.
